youtube.baslik: Central Auditory Disorders in Adults | Lesson 257 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Head injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis and neurodegenerative diseases can disrupt auditory processing even when the audiogram is normal. In this lesson we cover the main causes in adults, severe conditions such as cortical deafness and auditory agnosia, ABR findings in multiple sclerosis, adapting tests and teamwork.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: American Academy of Audiology, Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis, Treatment and Management of Children and Adults with Central Auditory Processing Disorder (2010); Musiek and Chermak, Handbook of Central Auditory Processing Disorder; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Hall, New Handbook of Auditory Evoked Responses; Gallun et al., Performance on tests of central auditory processing by individuals exposed to high-intensity blasts, Journal of Rehabilitation Research and Development (2012).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about auditory disorders in adults that develop after a disease or injury affecting the brain or brainstem.
We will cover head injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis, neurodegenerative diseases and teamwork in assessment.

maddeler.metin: Cognitive and language problems may coexist

cumleler: In adults, central auditory disorder is often linked to a specific event, such as head injury, stroke or neurological disease.
The person reports hearing and understanding without trouble before, then struggling, especially in noise, after the event.
Many central auditory tests were first developed and tested in adults with known lesion sites.
So adult assessment is relatively well suited to relating test results to the site of the lesion.
However, age-related peripheral loss can make results harder to interpret.
Cognitive problems, language disorders and fatigue can also affect test performance.
We can group the main causes of central auditory problems in adults into six groups.
Head injury follows an impact such as a traffic accident, a fall or a blast.
A stroke is a sudden disruption of blood supply to part of the brain; it can affect the auditory cortex or pathways.
Multiple sclerosis is a disease affecting the myelin sheath of nerve fibers, and it can also involve the auditory pathways.
In neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, auditory processing can also be affected.
Tumors along the auditory pathway, and their surgery, can also cause central auditory findings.
Temporal lobe epilepsy and surgery in this region are also among the groups assessed.
In head injury, the auditory system can be affected at both the peripheral and central levels.
Temporal bone fracture, eardrum perforation, ossicular chain disruption or inner ear concussion can cause peripheral loss.
Diffuse damage to brain tissue can affect the pathways between the brainstem and the cortex.
People most often complain of difficulty understanding speech in noise, oversensitivity to sound and tinnitus.
In soldiers exposed to blasts, central test abnormalities were reported more often, even with normal or mildly impaired audiograms.
This finding shows that a normal audiogram is not enough to explain listening complaints after an injury.
Central auditory findings can also appear after injuries considered mild.
The auditory cortex lies on the upper surface of the temporal lobe, within the lateral fissure.
A stroke in the vessels supplying this region can affect the auditory cortex and the nearby language areas.
In a unilateral cortical stroke, the audiogram often does not change, because each ear is represented in both hemispheres.
On dichotic tests, however, the score of the ear opposite the lesion often drops.
Sound localization, temporal processing and understanding in noise may also be impaired.
In left hemisphere strokes, involvement of Wernicke's area can impair speech comprehension; this overlaps with language disorder.
After a stroke, paralysis or speech disorder takes priority, so auditory complaints are often overlooked.
Cortical deafness usually results from damage to the auditory cortex on both sides, or to the pathways leading to it.
The person seems to barely respond to sounds; yet the auditory brainstem response is often normal.
This dissociation shows that the problem is not in the ear but above the brainstem.
Auditory agnosia is the inability to recognize what a sound is, despite noticing that it is there.
For example, the person hears a sound but cannot say whether it is a phone or a dog barking.
In pure word deafness, the person cannot understand speech, yet can read, write and recognize environmental sounds.
These conditions are rare, but they show very clearly that the audiogram alone does not assess the brain.
Multiple sclerosis is a disease affecting the myelin sheath of nerve fibers in the central nervous system.
When myelin is damaged, nerve conduction slows and the timing of signals is disrupted.
So the auditory brainstem response, or ABR, is often affected in people with plaques in the brainstem.

cumleler.yazi: In this example, wave I is at normal latency, but waves III and V are delayed; so the wave I to V interval is prolonged.
cumleler.ses: In this example, wave one is at normal latency, but waves three and five are delayed; so the wave one to five interval is prolonged.

cumleler: In some people the waves shrink or disappear; the person may describe difficulty understanding in noise.
Although rare, sudden hearing loss may be one of the first signs of the disease; in that case, medical evaluation is needed.

maddeler.metin: MLD and dichotic tests may be abnormal

cumleler: In people with multiple sclerosis, the most common auditory complaint is difficulty understanding speech in noise.
Complaints may vary with the relapse and remission phases of the disease.
With brainstem involvement, the masking level difference may shrink; dichotic and temporal tests may also be abnormal.
The pure tone audiogram, however, is often normal or appropriate for age.
Because fatigue is common in this disease, long test sessions can affect results negatively.
Findings are shared with the neurologist; auditory findings can contribute to monitoring the disease.

maddeler.metin: Hearing loss and cognitive decline link

cumleler: With age, the central auditory pathways also change; this is called central presbycusis.
Older adults may struggle more than their audiograms suggest, especially with fast speech and in noise.
Marked drops on dichotic tests have been reported in Alzheimer's disease and in older adults with memory problems.
The link between hearing loss and cognitive decline is one of the most researched topics in this field.
People with signs of memory or thinking problems are referred to a physician for appropriate cognitive assessment.
When choosing tests, remember that results of tasks with a heavy memory load will be affected by cognitive status.
The history covers the type and date of the neurological event, imaging findings, medications and the onset of the complaint.
Pure tone and speech tests, immittance, acoustic reflexes and otoacoustic emissions establish the peripheral status.
The auditory brainstem response and middle and late responses give objective information on the level at which the pathways are affected.
The central test battery includes dichotic, temporal pattern, gap detection and binaural tests.
Speech in noise tests and self-report scales show the person's difficulty in daily life.
Results are shared with neurology, neuropsychology and speech and language therapy to make a joint plan.
For people with aphasia, tests with a low language load are chosen instead of tests needing verbal responses.
In pattern tests, humming the pattern back or pointing to the answer partly gets around the language problem.
Because of fatigue and attention problems, sessions are kept short with frequent breaks.
In unilateral lesions, comparing the results of the two ears helps in thinking about the side of the lesion.
If there is age-related peripheral loss, levels are adjusted for it and results are interpreted together with thresholds.
Test results do not make a diagnosis on their own; they are considered with the neurological diagnosis and imaging.
As an example, consider a sixty-year-old who had a stroke in the right temporal lobe and cannot follow conversation in meetings.
The audiogram is appropriate for age, showing a symmetric, mild high-frequency loss in both ears.
On the dichotic digits test, the score of the left ear, opposite the lesion, is clearly low.
The person also struggles on a speech in noise test compared with peers; a self-report scale confirms the daily difficulty.
The team discusses a remote microphone, communication strategies and, if needed, auditory training.
This example shows that a normal or mildly impaired audiogram can hide a central difficulty in an adult.
Diagnosis and medical treatment are the neurologist's responsibility.
The neuropsychologist assesses memory, attention and other cognitive functions.
The speech and language therapist takes on rehabilitation of aphasia and communication difficulties.
The audiologist builds the auditory profile and plans auditory support.
Remote microphone systems and, if there is mild peripheral loss, well-fitted hearing aids can reduce listening load.
Family and friends are an important part of the process, with strategies such as face-to-face talk, less noise and slower speech.

sahneler.metin: Take the complaint "I hear but I don't understand" seriously after a neurological event. A normal audiogram does not rule out a central problem.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: take it seriously when someone says they hear but cannot understand after a stroke or head injury.
A normal or age-appropriate audiogram does not rule out a central auditory problem.
For these people, adding a speech in noise test and at least one dichotic or temporal test gives valuable information.
If there is a new sudden hearing loss or neurological sign, ask first for prompt medical evaluation instead of testing.

maddeler.metin: MS: ABR I to V interval _lengthens_

cumleler: In adults, central auditory disorders arise most often with head injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis and neurodegenerative disease.
In a unilateral cortical lesion, the audiogram is often normal; on dichotic tests, the opposite ear's score drops.
In multiple sclerosis, ABR waves may be delayed or lost; difficulty understanding in noise is common.
Assessment is adapted to language and cognitive status and carried out with neurology, neuropsychology and language therapy.

sahneler.soru: In cortical deafness, what is the auditory brainstem response usually like?
sahneler.aciklama: The damage is _above_ the brainstem; so the ABR is often normal.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in cortical deafness, what is the auditory brainstem response usually like?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: normal.
The damage is in the auditory cortex on both sides or the pathways to it; the pathway up to the brainstem is usually intact.
